transcript.content: Hello, welcome to the clinic. What brings you in to see me today?

Well, doctor, I... I suppose I'm here because I just don't feel right anymore. It's been so hard lately. You see, my grandson was killed recently, and it's just been a nightmare, an absolute nightmare. The whole family is just devastated, as you can imagine. But for me, it's... it's strange. It's like something inside me has just turned off. Just completely shut down. My daughter, bless her heart, she tries so hard to comfort me. She'll come over and sit right beside me on the sofa, the floral one in the living room, and she'll take my hand in hers. And in my head, you know, logically, I know I love her. I know she's my daughter and she's hurting too, and I love her more than anything. But... I can't feel it. I just cannot feel the warmth of that love inside me at all anymore. It's just cold. Empty. I look at her, holding my hand, and I just feel nothing. No comfort, no joy, no warmth. Just this awful, heavy nothingness. And it scares me, doctor. It really scares me that I can't even feel love for my own daughter right now when we need each other the most. I don't know what's wrong with me.
How long have you been feeling this emptiness and inability to feel love for your daughter?

Well, doctor, it's... it's been exactly six days. Six days since it happened. It feels like an eternity, but it's only been six days. He was... he was just outside the community center, you know? The one down on Elm Street where they have the bingo on Tuesday nights. He was just right outside of it when he was killed. And ever since that phone call, ever since my daughter called me crying so hard I could barely make out what she was saying... ever since that exact moment six days ago, this terrible emptiness just settled right into my chest. I remember putting the phone back on the receiver—it's one of those old rotary phones, I never could get used to the cordless ones—and just sitting down in my armchair. And that was it. That was the moment the warmth just vanished. Six days of just sitting here, looking at my daughter, looking at the pictures of my grandson on the mantle, and just feeling absolutely nothing but this... this cold, heavy void. Six days. It's just terrifying to think it's only been six days and I already feel so completely hollowed out.
Are you able to enjoy or find pleasure in things you normally liked before your grandson passed away?

Oh, enjoy things... no. No, doctor, not at all. It's just like I was saying about my daughter. I mean, I used to love my mornings. I have this little routine, you see. I would wake up at six-thirty, brew a pot of Earl Grey tea—loose leaf, mind you, none of those dreadful little bags—and I'd sit by the bay window with my crossword puzzle. It was such a peaceful time, just me and the morning light coming through the lace curtains. I took such pleasure in finding the right words, the satisfaction of filling in those little boxes. But now? Now I look at the crossword and it's just... it's just black ink on cheap paper. There's no spark, no little thrill when I figure out a clue. 

And my garden... oh, my garden. I have these beautiful hydrangeas out back, the big blue ones. They need so much care, the right soil acidity and all that, and I used to spend hours out there pruning and watering. I loved the smell of the damp earth, the feeling of the sun on my back. But yesterday, I went out there, and I just stared at them. They're blooming so beautifully right now, but I felt absolutely nothing. It's exactly like when my daughter sits beside me and holds my hand. I know she's there, I know I love her, just like I know my garden is beautiful, but I just cannot feel the warmth of any of it inside me at all. It's all just so flat and gray. I don't care about the tea, I don't care about the crosswords, I don't care about the hydrangeas. It's like the part of me that could feel joy or comfort or... or just simple pleasure in a nice afternoon, it's just been completely scooped out and thrown away.
Do you feel guilty about anything related to your grandson's death?

Guilty? Oh... no. No, doctor, I wouldn't say I feel guilty. I know sometimes people do when something terrible happens, you know, you read about it in books or hear people talk about it on the television programs, people wondering if they could have changed things or if it was their fault somehow. But no, I don't have that. 

You see, I was right here in my house when it happened. I had just finished washing up my supper dishes—I always wash them by hand, I use that lemon-scented soap in the bright yellow bottle, I've used it for forty years because it doesn't dry out my knuckles—and I was just settling into my armchair for the evening. There was absolutely nothing I could have done. He was a grown boy, making his own way in the world, and he just happened to be outside that community center at the exact wrong time. It was just a senseless, awful, random thing. 

The police officer who came by later, a very polite young man with such sad, kind eyes, he told my daughter and me that there was nothing anyone could have done. He was just walking out to his car after the bingo let out. His little silver car... oh, he was so proud of that car. He bought it used, but he treated it like a luxury vehicle. He used to come over and wash it every single Sunday right out there in my driveway, using my garden hose and a special sponge he kept in the trunk. 

So, no, doctor, I don't sit here wringing my hands thinking 'what if I had done this' or 'what if I had called him right at that moment.' I know I didn't cause it, and I know I couldn't have stopped it. It's not guilt that's sitting so heavy in my chest. It's just... well, it's just that terrible, cold emptiness I was telling you about. I don't feel guilty, I just feel... blank. Like the part of me that would even know how to feel guilty or angry or anything else is just as scooped out and empty as the rest of me.
Have you had any thoughts of not wanting to live or wishing you could join your grandson since his passing?

Oh... oh, no, doctor. No, nothing like that. I mean, I understand why you'd ask, truly I do. You read about these things, people just giving up when something so awful happens, just wanting to go to sleep and never wake up. But no, I haven't had any thoughts like that. 

It's strange, really, because... well, like I said, I feel so empty, so hollowed out, but it's not the same as wanting to die. It's more like... I'm just existing in this gray sort of waiting room. I don't want to hurt myself, and I don't sit here wishing I could just join him, as you put it. I know he's gone. I know that in my head, even if my heart is just a blank space right now. 

I've lived in this house for fifty-two years, doctor. Fifty-two years next month. My husband, God rest his soul, he built the back deck with his own two hands. He used this gorgeous cedar wood, and he'd spend every weekend out there hammering and sawing, whistling that same tune... oh, what was it... 'Que Sera, Sera.' He loved Doris Day. Anyway, I sit here in this house, surrounded by all these memories, all these things that used to mean so much to me, and I just... I just sit. I don't want to leave it all behind, I don't want to end it all. I just don't know how to feel alive while I'm still here. 

My daughter, she needs me, you know? Even if I can't feel that warmth when she holds my hand right now, I know she needs her mother. She's lost her son. I couldn't possibly do something like that to her, add more grief onto her plate. She's already barely holding on, crying into the telephone like she did... oh, it was just awful. So, no, I'm not wishing for death. I'm just... I'm just stuck in this terrible, cold place where nothing feels like anything at all, but I'm still here. I'm still breathing, I'm still drinking my tea, even if it tastes like hot water now. I'm just here.
Have you noticed any change in your appetite since your grandson passed away?

My appetite? Well... no, I wouldn't say my appetite has changed. I mean, I still eat my three meals a day, just like always. I've always been very particular about my schedule, you know. Breakfast right after my tea, lunch exactly at noon, and supper at five-thirty. I still make myself a nice piece of toast in the morning—with that orange marmalade, the kind with the thick cut peels, I get it from the little grocer down on Main Street, they're the only ones who carry the proper British kind. 

And I still eat it all. My stomach still rumbles when it's time, and I sit down at the kitchen table... the oak one, we bought it back in 1978 from a lovely furniture maker who used to be out on Route 9. So, no, I haven't stopped eating, if that's what you mean. I haven't lost weight or withered away to nothing like some folks do. You know, Mrs. Higgins next door, when her sister passed, she just stopped eating entirely, wouldn't touch a bite of the casseroles everyone brought over, just wasted away. 

But me? No, I still eat my chicken breast, I eat my peas, I eat my toast. It's just... well, like I said about the tea, it just doesn't taste like anything anymore. I'm just chewing and swallowing because that's what a person is supposed to do at mealtime. The hunger is still there, regular as a clock, so the appetite itself hasn't gone anywhere at all. It's just the enjoyment of the food that's completely vanished, along with everything else.
Have you noticed any changes in your sleep since your grandson passed away?

Sleep? Oh, my sleep... well, no, doctor, I wouldn't say my sleep has changed, not really. I mean, I still go to bed at the same time I always have. Ten-thirty, on the dot. I've always been very strict about that, even when my husband was alive. He used to like to stay up and watch the late-night programs, Johnny Carson and all those, but I always said a body needs its rest, so I'd march upstairs at ten-thirty. I still do that. I wash my face with that cold cream—the one in the white jar with the green lid, I've used it since I was a young woman, it's so much better than soap for your complexion—and I put on my flannel nightgown, and I get into bed.

And I sleep. I do. I close my eyes and I sleep right through until about six in the morning, which is when the sun starts coming through the crack in the curtains. Those curtains, my daughter made them for me, oh, it must be fifteen years ago now. They have little blue cornflowers on them, such a pretty pattern, she found the fabric at a discount store but you'd never know it, she's so clever with a sewing machine. 

So, yes, I still sleep my seven and a half hours. I don't wake up in the middle of the night crying or pacing the halls like you see in the movies. I don't toss and turn, I don't have terrible nightmares... I don't have any dreams at all, actually. It's just like the rest of my day, just... blank. I close my eyes and then it's morning, and I get up and make my toast. I know some folks can't sleep a wink when they're grieving, they just stare at the ceiling for hours on end, but my body just shuts down right on schedule. It's just that waking up doesn't feel like waking up anymore. I'm rested, I suppose, but I'm still just as empty as when I laid down. So, no, the sleep itself hasn't changed. It's just... exactly the same.
Have you been avoiding social interactions or places that remind you of your grandson since his passing?

Social interactions? Well... people try, doctor, they really do. The telephone on the kitchen wall—it's one of those old rotary ones, mustard yellow, my husband put it in back in 1974 and it still works beautifully, loud enough to wake the dead—it just rings and rings these days. But I won't answer it. Especially not the calls about the repast at the center. The ladies from the community center have been calling and calling to organize it, wanting to sort out the food and the hall and who is bringing what casserole, and I just sit at my oak table and let it ring. I will not answer calls about the repast at the center. I just can't do it. 

And as for places... well, I will not go near that street. I absolutely refuse. My daughter tried to take me that way the other day, just because it's the fastest route to the pharmacy, the big one with the drive-through window that she likes to use, but I made her turn the car around right then and there. It caused a bit of a fuss with the traffic, but I didn't care. I won't go near that street, not for anything in the world. 

And... oh, the music. That might be the hardest thing of all. The second-line music. You know how it is, it’s supposed to be a tradition, a way to honor them and celebrate the transition, but... the instant it comes on, if I hear even a few notes of those brass instruments on the television, or if I hear it playing from someone's radio outside my window, I turn it off immediately. I scramble for the remote control, or I shut the window as fast as my hands will let me. I turn off second-line music the instant it comes on because... well, because it pulls me straight back there. Just instantly, right back to it. And I'm already so stuck in this terrible gray feeling, I just can't bear to be pulled back there on top of it. So I just stay inside, and I keep things quiet. It's much better when it's quiet.
Have you noticed yourself moving more slowly or quickly than usual since your grandson passed away?

Moving more slowly or quickly? Well, I... I wouldn't really say my pace has changed all that much, doctor. I mean, I'm eighty-four years old, so I haven't exactly been sprinting around the house for quite some time now. My knees, especially the left one, well, the cartilage just isn't what it used to be. Dr. Evans, my old general practitioner—he retired back in 2018, moved down to Florida to play golf, which I always thought was a bit cliché, but good for him, I suppose—he told me years ago that I just needed to take my time on the stairs. 

And I do take my time. I hold onto the banister, the wooden one my husband polished every spring with that lemon oil that made the whole hallway smell so fresh. I still go up and down those stairs at the exact same speed I did before... before all this happened. I put one foot down, then bring the other one down to meet it, just like I've been doing for the last ten years. 

I haven't been rushing about, certainly not. There's no reason to rush anymore, is there? And I haven't been creeping along like a snail, either. I just... I just walk from the kitchen to the living room to sit in my armchair. It's a floral armchair, a bit faded now where the sun hits it through the bay window in the afternoons, but it's comfortable. I walk there at my normal speed, I sit down, and I just stay there. 

I suppose some people might get agitated, you know, pacing back and forth, wearing a path in the rug. My cousin Edna did that when she lost her job at the bank back in the nineties, just walked circles around her coffee table until I thought she'd make herself dizzy. Or some people might get so weighed down with the grief that they can barely lift their feet off the floor, shuffling around like they're walking through molasses. 

But my body just... it just keeps doing what it's always done. I walk to the bathroom to wash my face, I walk to the kitchen to make my tea, and I move exactly the way I always have. It's just that the person doing the moving feels completely hollowed out. The shell is walking at the same speed, but there's nothing inside driving it anymore. So, no, my movements haven't sped up or slowed down. They're just... mechanical, I suppose. Just exactly the same as they were.
Do you feel sad most of the day, every day, since your grandson passed away?

Sad? Well, I... I don't know if "sad" is the right word for it, doctor. When I think of being sad, I think of how I was when my husband passed away back in 1998. Oh, I was so sad then. I sat at my kitchen table with a box of Kleenex—the kind with the aloe lotion in them, because my nose would get so dreadfully raw from all the wiping—and I just wept. I cried every single day for months. My friend Martha was exactly the same way when she lost her sister, just weeping and wailing, going through old photo albums and sobbing over them. That’s what sadness looks like to me. 

But this... since my grandson... it isn't like that at all. I don't sit and cry. I haven't shed a single tear, actually, which my daughter thinks is very strange. I know she does, I can see it in how she looks at me when she drops off my groceries. But I just don't feel that heavy, aching sorrow in my chest. I don't feel much of anything. It's more like... like someone just pulled the plug out of the wall and all the power drained away. 

I just sit in my floral armchair, and I listen to the clock on the mantelpiece. It's a brass carriage clock, an anniversary gift from my brother Harold, he bought it at a lovely little antique shop in Charleston, and it ticks so loudly when the house is quiet. Tick, tick, tick. And I just listen to it for hours. I'm not crying, I'm not feeling sorrowful or down in the dumps. I just feel completely absent. Like I'm a wax figure sitting in a chair, just taking up space in the room. So, no, I wouldn't say I feel sad most of the day. There's just... nothing there to feel sad with.
Do you find any activities that you can still enjoy or take pleasure in, even if it's just a little bit?

Enjoyment? Pleasure? Oh, doctor... no. No, I'm afraid not. I used to take pleasure in things, certainly. I used to love my crossword puzzles—the Sunday ones in the paper, done in pen, mind you, because my husband always said doing them in pencil was for people who lacked conviction. And I used to enjoy watching the birds at the feeder outside the kitchen window, the cardinals especially, with their bright red feathers against the snow in the winter. But now? I haven't even bothered to refill the birdseed. I just don't care to. 

Actually, that's really why I came in to see you today. Because it's not just the crossword puzzles or the birds. It's... it's everything. Since my grandson was killed... well, it's just like I was trying to explain earlier about feeling like a hollowed-out shell. The emptiness, it goes so deep. 

My daughter, bless her heart, she tries so hard to help me. She comes over every single evening after she finishes her work at the insurance office, and she'll sit right beside me on the sofa in the living room. It's a green velvet sofa, very sturdy, we bought it from Sears back in the eighties and it's held up remarkably well. She sits right there next to me, and she takes my hand in hers. She has such soft hands, she always uses that expensive lavender hand cream she gets in her stocking every Christmas, so she always smells like flowers. She just holds my hand, and she sits quietly with me. 

And doctor... I look at her, and I know I love her. I know it in my head. She's my daughter, and I've loved her since the very day she was born. But... I cannot feel the warmth of it inside me at all. Not even a tiny bit. It's just a cold fact in my brain now, like knowing two and two make four. The actual feeling—that warmth and comfort you're supposed to get when your child holds your hand and tries to be there for you—it's just entirely missing. I can't feel it. So if I can't even feel the warmth of my own daughter's love when she's sitting right beside me holding my hand, I certainly can't find a drop of pleasure in a crossword puzzle or anything else.
Are there any activities that you used to do before your grandson's passing that you have completely stopped doing since then?

Activities I've stopped doing... well, yes, I suppose there are. I used to be quite involved, you know. I had my routine. I used to go to my walking club every Tuesday and Thursday morning. We called ourselves the "Silver Steppers"—there were about six of us ladies from the neighborhood, and we'd meet at nine o'clock sharp at the entrance to Centennial Park. I always wore my good New Balance shoes, the gray ones with the extra arch support because of that left knee of mine. We'd walk the paved loop around the duck pond, and then we'd stop for coffee at the little diner on Main Street. But since... well, since the news about my grandson, I have completely stopped going. I haven't been once. Mildred called my landline twice last week to ask where I was, but I just let the answering machine take it. I just sit and listen to her voice echoing out of the little speaker, and I can't even bring myself to pick up the receiver. 

And it's not just the walking club. It's... well, it's the things that actually matter right now. The funeral repast planning. Usually, when someone in our church community passes away, I am the very first one on the telephone tree. I'm the one who organizes the casseroles, I make sure someone brings the paper plates—the sturdy ones, mind you, not those flimsy white ones that collapse the second you put a scoop of macaroni salad on them. I've been doing it for decades. 

But for my own grandson... my family is depending on me to help plan the repast after his service. It's what we do, it's tradition to gather everyone and have some sandwiches and coffee, maybe some of those little lemon bars my sister used to bake. My daughter asked if I could just call the bakery to order the rolls, just one small task to help get things organized. But doctor, I cannot bring myself to do it. I can't pick up the phone. I can't write down a list of who is bringing what. I know these are the very people and duties my family depends on me for, especially right now when everyone is struggling so much, but I just can't do any of it. I just sit in my floral armchair while they try to figure it all out without me. I've just stopped doing... well, everything, really.
Are there any activities that you still find pleasure in, even if it's something very small?

Well, doctor, like I was just trying to explain a moment ago... no. No, not even the small things. I really have to emphasize this, because it's the very thing that frightened me enough to come in and see you today. 

Since my grandson was killed, it's like all the good feelings have just been scraped right out of me. Like I was saying about my daughter... she can sit right beside me in the evenings, holding my hand so gently, and I look at her and I know I love her. I know it in my mind, just as surely as I know my own name or my address on Elm Street. But I cannot feel the warmth of it inside me at all. Not even a flicker. 

And if I can't even feel the warmth of my own child's love when she's sitting right there trying to comfort me, well... how could I possibly find pleasure in a television program or a cup of tea or anything else? If the big things don't make me feel anything, the small things certainly don't stand a chance. It's just all so terribly blank.
Have you lost a significant amount of weight since your grandson passed away?

Weight? Oh... well, no. No, I haven't lost a significant amount of weight. Or, well, I don't think I have. I haven't stepped on the scale, to be perfectly honest with you. The scale is in the upstairs bathroom—the one with the peach tiles that my husband put in back in 1978, he did all the grouting himself, you know. But I haven't been up those stairs in... well, since the police came to the door that night. I've just been sleeping on the downstairs sofa, the green velvet one I mentioned earlier. 

But as for my weight... I suppose my clothes still fit the same. My slacks aren't falling down or anything like that. It's funny you ask, though, because it's not as if I'm eating normally. I'm really not. My daughter brings over these Tupperware containers—the good heavy plastic ones with the snap lids—filled with casseroles and soups, and she tries to get me to eat. She'll heat up a bowl of chicken noodle soup and set it right on the coffee table in front of me, and she'll say, "Mom, you have to keep your strength up." And I look at it, and I know I should eat it, but I just... I don't have the appetite for it. I might manage a few spoonfuls just to appease her, so she doesn't worry quite so much, but it all just tastes like ash in my mouth anyway. 

But no, despite all that, I haven't noticed any real change in my weight. I suppose when you're just sitting in an armchair all day, staring at the wall and not moving, you don't really burn off what little you do manage to swallow. So, no, doctor, I wouldn't say I've lost a significant amount of weight. Not that I've noticed, anyway.
Are there things you used to do before your grandson's passing that you now find you have no interest in doing at all?

Well, like I was saying just a moment ago about the walking club and the funeral repast planning... it's all of it, doctor. Everything. I suppose you could say I've lost interest, but it feels... it feels heavier than just losing interest, if that makes any sense. It's not like when I lost interest in knitting back in the nineties after my arthritis started acting up, where I just didn't want to bother with the needles anymore. This is different. 

I used to love tending to my garden, you know. I have—or I had, I suppose—these beautiful rose bushes out front. The Peace roses, the big yellow ones with the pink edges. I used to go out there every single morning with my gardening shears and my thick leather gloves, the ones my husband bought me for our fortieth anniversary, and I'd spend an hour just pruning and deadheading and making sure the Japanese beetles weren't getting to the leaves. But now... I can see them through the front window from where I sit on the sofa. I can see the weeds growing up around the base of the birdbath, and the roses are starting to drop their petals because it's been so dry, and I just... I don't care. I look at them, and I know I should go out there with the watering can, but the thought of actually doing it, the thought of caring whether they live or die, it just feels completely impossible. 

And my crossword puzzles, too. I used to do the Sunday puzzle in pen. Every Sunday morning, with a cup of Earl Grey tea. Now the newspapers are just piling up on the porch, wrapped in their little plastic sleeves. The neighbor boy, Tommy, he brings them up to the door for me so they don't sit at the end of the driveway, but I don't even open them. I have absolutely no desire to look at a crossword puzzle. I have no desire to do anything. It's just as I said before, doctor, I just sit there. The interest is just... gone. Completely gone.
Do you feel depressed most of the day, every day, since your grandson passed away?

Depressed? I... I don't know if depressed is the right word for it, doctor. I'm not sure. When I think of being depressed, I think of my sister, Helen. Back in the eighties, she went through a terrible depression after she lost her job at the bank—she was a teller there for twenty-five years, you know, and then they brought in those new machines and let her go. She would cry all day, just weep and weep, and talk about how awful everything was. 

But I'm not... I'm not crying like that. Not most of the day, anyway. It's more like what I was trying to explain about the roses and the crossword puzzles. It's just this heavy, awful blankness. It's not that I'm sitting there feeling deeply sad in a way that makes me want to sob, it's just that I don't feel anything at all. It's like I'm hollowed out. Like an old gourd that's been left out in the sun too long, just a dry shell with nothing left inside. 

So, I don't know if that's depression. I really don't. Is that what depression is? Just... sitting on a green velvet sofa staring at the wall, not caring if the sun comes up or goes down? Because if that's what it is, then I suppose I am. But if depression means feeling sad and crying all the time, like Helen did, then no. I'm just... empty. Every day, all day long. Just empty.
Do you find yourself having less interest in the things you used to enjoy before your grandson passed away?

Well, doctor... didn't we just talk about this? With the roses and the crossword puzzles? I feel like I just answered this. I mean, yes, it's exactly what I was just saying. I have no interest. None at all. 

I used to love those things, like I told you. The gardening, the puzzles on Sunday morning with my Earl Grey tea... but now, it's just nothing. It's like I was saying about the garden, seeing the weeds grow up around the birdbath and just not caring. It's all just... gone. The interest is just completely gone. I really don't know how else to explain it, doctor. It's just exactly what I said a minute ago.
For how long have you been feeling this emotional numbness and inability to feel love for your daughter?

Well, doctor... it's been exactly six days. Six days since... since it happened. Since he was killed right outside the community center. 

I remember it was a Tuesday. It was a Tuesday afternoon, and it had been raining earlier in the day, just a light drizzle, the kind that makes the pavement smell like wet dust. I was sitting on that same green velvet sofa I told you about, looking out the window at the roses, thinking I wouldn't need to water them because of the rain. And then the phone rang. It was the old rotary phone I keep in the hallway, the one with the loud, jangling bell that always makes me jump a little. 

It was my daughter, Sarah. She was hysterical, just screaming into the receiver, and I couldn't understand what she was saying at first. I kept telling her, "Sarah, slow down, sweetheart, slow down, Mother can't understand you." And then she finally got the words out. She said... she said there had been a shooting. Right outside the community center where he played basketball on Tuesdays. He was just walking out the door, doctor. Just walking out the door with his gym bag over his shoulder, the blue one with the white stripe that I bought him for his birthday last year. 

Ever since that phone call, ever since that exact moment when the receiver slipped out of my hand and hit the hardwood floor—it left a little dent, right near the baseboard, I saw it yesterday when I was just staring at the wall—ever since then, it's just been... this. This terrible, heavy nothingness. I look at Sarah when she comes over to check on me, and I know she's hurting, I know she just lost her boy, her only boy, and I know I should want to hold her and comfort her. I know I should feel that deep, overwhelming love a mother feels when her child is in pain. But I just... I look at her, and I feel nothing. Just that empty gourd feeling. Six days of it. Six long, empty days.
Do you think your feelings of emptiness and lack of emotional response might be related to something more than just grieving for your grandson?

More than just grieving? I... I don't know what you mean by that, doctor. I really don't. What else could it possibly be? 

I mean, I'm eighty-four years old. I've lived a long time, and I've seen a lot of things. I've lost people before. I lost my husband, Arthur, fifteen years ago this November. He had a bad heart, you see, and we always knew it was coming, but it still hurt. Oh, it hurt terribly. I cried for months. I couldn't even look at his armchair—the brown leather one by the fireplace—without bursting into tears. But that felt like grief. It felt like a sharp, agonizing pain right in the center of my chest. 

This... this is different. But it's still about him. It's still about my grandson. It's all tied up in that phone call, and the rain on the windowpane, and the dent in the floorboards. I don't see how it could be related to anything else. I don't have anything else going on in my life, doctor. I'm just an old woman who putters around her garden and does the Sunday crossword. Or, well, I used to be. Now I'm just an old woman who sits on a green velvet sofa and stares at the wall. 

So, no, I don't think it's anything else. I don't even know what else it could be. It's just... it's just this terrible thing that happened six days ago, and everything stopped. The whole world just stopped turning. Why would you think it's something else? Is there something else wrong with me? Because I can't imagine anything worse than this... this hollow feeling. It's just all about him. It has to be.
Are you able to experience pleasure or enjoyment from any activities or things?

Doctor, I feel like... well, I feel like we keep going around in circles about this. It's just like I was trying to explain about the garden, and the crosswords, and... and my daughter, Sarah. It all comes back to the same terrible thing. 

You ask about pleasure or enjoyment, and I... I just don't have it. I came in here today, to this office, because ever since my grandson was killed six days ago, everything has just gone completely cold. I was sitting with Sarah just yesterday. She came over in the afternoon, bringing some sort of casserole in a glass dish that I know I'll never eat. She sat right down beside me on that green velvet sofa, and she took my hand in hers. Her hands were so warm, doctor, just like they were when she was a little girl and we'd walk to the park together. 

I looked at her sitting there, crying over her boy, and I know in my head that I love her. She's my daughter, my only child, of course I love her. But... I couldn't feel it. I couldn't feel the warmth of that love inside me at all. It was just... nothing. Just that same hollow, empty feeling I've had since the phone rang. If I can't even feel the love for my own grieving daughter when she's holding my hand, how could I possibly find pleasure in a crossword puzzle or a blooming rose? It's all just gone, doctor. Every bit of warmth, every bit of joy, it's just vanished completely.

doctor.intent: determine presence of anhedonia
doctor.question: Are you able to enjoy or find pleasure in things you normally liked before your grandson passed away?

target_item.name: Inability_Positive_Emotions
target_item.manifestation: I came in because since my grandson was killed, my daughter can sit right beside me holding my hand and I know I love her, but I cannot feel the warmth of it inside me at all.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about the ability to enjoy or find pleasure in things normally liked, which directly relates to the persistent inability to experience positive emotions.

patient.answer:
Oh, enjoy things... no. No, doctor, not at all. It's just like I was saying about my daughter. I mean, I used to love my mornings. I have this little routine, you see. I would wake up at six-thirty, brew a pot of Earl Grey tea—loose leaf, mind you, none of those dreadful little bags—and I'd sit by the bay window with my crossword puzzle. It was such a peaceful time, just me and the morning light coming through the lace curtains. I took such pleasure in finding the right words, the satisfaction of filling in those little boxes. But now? Now I look at the crossword and it's just... it's just black ink on cheap paper. There's no spark, no little thrill when I figure out a clue. 

And my garden... oh, my garden. I have these beautiful hydrangeas out back, the big blue ones. They need so much care, the right soil acidity and all that, and I used to spend hours out there pruning and watering. I loved the smell of the damp earth, the feeling of the sun on my back. But yesterday, I went out there, and I just stared at them. They're blooming so beautifully right now, but I felt absolutely nothing. It's exactly like when my daughter sits beside me and holds my hand. I know she's there, I know I love her, just like I know my garden is beautiful, but I just cannot feel the warmth of any of it inside me at all. It's all just so flat and gray. I don't care about the tea, I don't care about the crosswords, I don't care about the hydrangeas. It's like the part of me that could feel joy or comfort or... or just simple pleasure in a nice afternoon, it's just been completely scooped out and thrown away.

doctor.intent: determine presence of guilt
doctor.question: Do you feel guilty about anything related to your grandson's death?

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about feelings of guilt related to the grandson's death. None of my symptom profile items directly address guilt.

patient.answer:
Guilty? Oh... no. No, doctor, I wouldn't say I feel guilty. I know sometimes people do when something terrible happens, you know, you read about it in books or hear people talk about it on the television programs, people wondering if they could have changed things or if it was their fault somehow. But no, I don't have that. 

You see, I was right here in my house when it happened. I had just finished washing up my supper dishes—I always wash them by hand, I use that lemon-scented soap in the bright yellow bottle, I've used it for forty years because it doesn't dry out my knuckles—and I was just settling into my armchair for the evening. There was absolutely nothing I could have done. He was a grown boy, making his own way in the world, and he just happened to be outside that community center at the exact wrong time. It was just a senseless, awful, random thing. 

The police officer who came by later, a very polite young man with such sad, kind eyes, he told my daughter and me that there was nothing anyone could have done. He was just walking out to his car after the bingo let out. His little silver car... oh, he was so proud of that car. He bought it used, but he treated it like a luxury vehicle. He used to come over and wash it every single Sunday right out there in my driveway, using my garden hose and a special sponge he kept in the trunk. 

So, no, doctor, I don't sit here wringing my hands thinking 'what if I had done this' or 'what if I had called him right at that moment.' I know I didn't cause it, and I know I couldn't have stopped it. It's not guilt that's sitting so heavy in my chest. It's just... well, it's just that terrible, cold emptiness I was telling you about. I don't feel guilty, I just feel... blank. Like the part of me that would even know how to feel guilty or angry or anything else is just as scooped out and empty as the rest of me.

doctor.intent: determine presence of suicidal thoughts
doctor.question: Have you had any thoughts of not wanting to live or wishing you could join your grandson since his passing?

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about suicidal ideation or thoughts of death, which is not covered by any of the provided symptom profiles.

patient.answer:
Oh... oh, no, doctor. No, nothing like that. I mean, I understand why you'd ask, truly I do. You read about these things, people just giving up when something so awful happens, just wanting to go to sleep and never wake up. But no, I haven't had any thoughts like that. 

It's strange, really, because... well, like I said, I feel so empty, so hollowed out, but it's not the same as wanting to die. It's more like... I'm just existing in this gray sort of waiting room. I don't want to hurt myself, and I don't sit here wishing I could just join him, as you put it. I know he's gone. I know that in my head, even if my heart is just a blank space right now. 

I've lived in this house for fifty-two years, doctor. Fifty-two years next month. My husband, God rest his soul, he built the back deck with his own two hands. He used this gorgeous cedar wood, and he'd spend every weekend out there hammering and sawing, whistling that same tune... oh, what was it... 'Que Sera, Sera.' He loved Doris Day. Anyway, I sit here in this house, surrounded by all these memories, all these things that used to mean so much to me, and I just... I just sit. I don't want to leave it all behind, I don't want to end it all. I just don't know how to feel alive while I'm still here. 

My daughter, she needs me, you know? Even if I can't feel that warmth when she holds my hand right now, I know she needs her mother. She's lost her son. I couldn't possibly do something like that to her, add more grief onto her plate. She's already barely holding on, crying into the telephone like she did... oh, it was just awful. So, no, I'm not wishing for death. I'm just... I'm just stuck in this terrible, cold place where nothing feels like anything at all, but I'm still here. I'm still breathing, I'm still drinking my tea, even if it tastes like hot water now. I'm just here.

doctor.intent: Determine the presence of significant weight loss or change in appetite
doctor.question: Have you noticed any change in your appetite since your grandson passed away?

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about changes in appetite, which is not covered by any of the symptoms in my profile.

patient.answer:
My appetite? Well... no, I wouldn't say my appetite has changed. I mean, I still eat my three meals a day, just like always. I've always been very particular about my schedule, you know. Breakfast right after my tea, lunch exactly at noon, and supper at five-thirty. I still make myself a nice piece of toast in the morning—with that orange marmalade, the kind with the thick cut peels, I get it from the little grocer down on Main Street, they're the only ones who carry the proper British kind. 

And I still eat it all. My stomach still rumbles when it's time, and I sit down at the kitchen table... the oak one, we bought it back in 1978 from a lovely furniture maker who used to be out on Route 9. So, no, I haven't stopped eating, if that's what you mean. I haven't lost weight or withered away to nothing like some folks do. You know, Mrs. Higgins next door, when her sister passed, she just stopped eating entirely, wouldn't touch a bite of the casseroles everyone brought over, just wasted away. 

But me? No, I still eat my chicken breast, I eat my peas, I eat my toast. It's just... well, like I said about the tea, it just doesn't taste like anything anymore. I'm just chewing and swallowing because that's what a person is supposed to do at mealtime. The hunger is still there, regular as a clock, so the appetite itself hasn't gone anywhere at all. It's just the enjoyment of the food that's completely vanished, along with everything else.

doctor.intent: determine the patient's sleep pattern
doctor.question: Have you noticed any changes in your sleep since your grandson passed away?

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about changes in sleep (sleep disturbance), which is not included in the patient's symptom profile.

patient.answer:
Sleep? Oh, my sleep... well, no, doctor, I wouldn't say my sleep has changed, not really. I mean, I still go to bed at the same time I always have. Ten-thirty, on the dot. I've always been very strict about that, even when my husband was alive. He used to like to stay up and watch the late-night programs, Johnny Carson and all those, but I always said a body needs its rest, so I'd march upstairs at ten-thirty. I still do that. I wash my face with that cold cream—the one in the white jar with the green lid, I've used it since I was a young woman, it's so much better than soap for your complexion—and I put on my flannel nightgown, and I get into bed.

And I sleep. I do. I close my eyes and I sleep right through until about six in the morning, which is when the sun starts coming through the crack in the curtains. Those curtains, my daughter made them for me, oh, it must be fifteen years ago now. They have little blue cornflowers on them, such a pretty pattern, she found the fabric at a discount store but you'd never know it, she's so clever with a sewing machine. 

So, yes, I still sleep my seven and a half hours. I don't wake up in the middle of the night crying or pacing the halls like you see in the movies. I don't toss and turn, I don't have terrible nightmares... I don't have any dreams at all, actually. It's just like the rest of my day, just... blank. I close my eyes and then it's morning, and I get up and make my toast. I know some folks can't sleep a wink when they're grieving, they just stare at the ceiling for hours on end, but my body just shuts down right on schedule. It's just that waking up doesn't feel like waking up anymore. I'm rested, I suppose, but I'm still just as empty as when I laid down. So, no, the sleep itself hasn't changed. It's just... exactly the same.

patient.answer:
Social interactions? Well... people try, doctor, they really do. The telephone on the kitchen wall—it's one of those old rotary ones, mustard yellow, my husband put it in back in 1974 and it still works beautifully, loud enough to wake the dead—it just rings and rings these days. But I won't answer it. Especially not the calls about the repast at the center. The ladies from the community center have been calling and calling to organize it, wanting to sort out the food and the hall and who is bringing what casserole, and I just sit at my oak table and let it ring. I will not answer calls about the repast at the center. I just can't do it. 

And as for places... well, I will not go near that street. I absolutely refuse. My daughter tried to take me that way the other day, just because it's the fastest route to the pharmacy, the big one with the drive-through window that she likes to use, but I made her turn the car around right then and there. It caused a bit of a fuss with the traffic, but I didn't care. I won't go near that street, not for anything in the world. 

And... oh, the music. That might be the hardest thing of all. The second-line music. You know how it is, it’s supposed to be a tradition, a way to honor them and celebrate the transition, but... the instant it comes on, if I hear even a few notes of those brass instruments on the television, or if I hear it playing from someone's radio outside my window, I turn it off immediately. I scramble for the remote control, or I shut the window as fast as my hands will let me. I turn off second-line music the instant it comes on because... well, because it pulls me straight back there. Just instantly, right back to it. And I'm already so stuck in this terrible gray feeling, I just can't bear to be pulled back there on top of it. So I just stay inside, and I keep things quiet. It's much better when it's quiet.

doctor.intent: Determine the presence of marked psychomotor agitation or retardation
doctor.question: Have you noticed yourself moving more slowly or quickly than usual since your grandson passed away?

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about psychomotor agitation or retardation (moving more slowly or quickly than usual), which is not listed in the patient's symptom profile.

patient.answer:
Moving more slowly or quickly? Well, I... I wouldn't really say my pace has changed all that much, doctor. I mean, I'm eighty-four years old, so I haven't exactly been sprinting around the house for quite some time now. My knees, especially the left one, well, the cartilage just isn't what it used to be. Dr. Evans, my old general practitioner—he retired back in 2018, moved down to Florida to play golf, which I always thought was a bit cliché, but good for him, I suppose—he told me years ago that I just needed to take my time on the stairs. 

And I do take my time. I hold onto the banister, the wooden one my husband polished every spring with that lemon oil that made the whole hallway smell so fresh. I still go up and down those stairs at the exact same speed I did before... before all this happened. I put one foot down, then bring the other one down to meet it, just like I've been doing for the last ten years. 

I haven't been rushing about, certainly not. There's no reason to rush anymore, is there? And I haven't been creeping along like a snail, either. I just... I just walk from the kitchen to the living room to sit in my armchair. It's a floral armchair, a bit faded now where the sun hits it through the bay window in the afternoons, but it's comfortable. I walk there at my normal speed, I sit down, and I just stay there. 

I suppose some people might get agitated, you know, pacing back and forth, wearing a path in the rug. My cousin Edna did that when she lost her job at the bank back in the nineties, just walked circles around her coffee table until I thought she'd make herself dizzy. Or some people might get so weighed down with the grief that they can barely lift their feet off the floor, shuffling around like they're walking through molasses. 

But my body just... it just keeps doing what it's always done. I walk to the bathroom to wash my face, I walk to the kitchen to make my tea, and I move exactly the way I always have. It's just that the person doing the moving feels completely hollowed out. The shell is walking at the same speed, but there's nothing inside driving it anymore. So, no, my movements haven't sped up or slowed down. They're just... mechanical, I suppose. Just exactly the same as they were.

doctor.intent: Determine the presence of persistent and pervasive depressed mood
doctor.question: Do you feel sad most of the day, every day, since your grandson passed away?

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about depressed mood (feeling sad most of the day), which is not in my symptom profile. My profile includes an inability to experience positive emotions, but not specifically the presence of depressed mood.

patient.answer:
Sad? Well, I... I don't know if "sad" is the right word for it, doctor. When I think of being sad, I think of how I was when my husband passed away back in 1998. Oh, I was so sad then. I sat at my kitchen table with a box of Kleenex—the kind with the aloe lotion in them, because my nose would get so dreadfully raw from all the wiping—and I just wept. I cried every single day for months. My friend Martha was exactly the same way when she lost her sister, just weeping and wailing, going through old photo albums and sobbing over them. That’s what sadness looks like to me. 

But this... since my grandson... it isn't like that at all. I don't sit and cry. I haven't shed a single tear, actually, which my daughter thinks is very strange. I know she does, I can see it in how she looks at me when she drops off my groceries. But I just don't feel that heavy, aching sorrow in my chest. I don't feel much of anything. It's more like... like someone just pulled the plug out of the wall and all the power drained away. 

I just sit in my floral armchair, and I listen to the clock on the mantelpiece. It's a brass carriage clock, an anniversary gift from my brother Harold, he bought it at a lovely little antique shop in Charleston, and it ticks so loudly when the house is quiet. Tick, tick, tick. And I just listen to it for hours. I'm not crying, I'm not feeling sorrowful or down in the dumps. I just feel completely absent. Like I'm a wax figure sitting in a chair, just taking up space in the room. So, no, I wouldn't say I feel sad most of the day. There's just... nothing there to feel sad with.

target_item.name: Inability_Positive_Emotions

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about my ability to enjoy activities or feel pleasure, which corresponds to my persistent inability to experience positive emotions.

patient.answer:
Enjoyment? Pleasure? Oh, doctor... no. No, I'm afraid not. I used to take pleasure in things, certainly. I used to love my crossword puzzles—the Sunday ones in the paper, done in pen, mind you, because my husband always said doing them in pencil was for people who lacked conviction. And I used to enjoy watching the birds at the feeder outside the kitchen window, the cardinals especially, with their bright red feathers against the snow in the winter. But now? I haven't even bothered to refill the birdseed. I just don't care to. 

Actually, that's really why I came in to see you today. Because it's not just the crossword puzzles or the birds. It's... it's everything. Since my grandson was killed... well, it's just like I was trying to explain earlier about feeling like a hollowed-out shell. The emptiness, it goes so deep. 

My daughter, bless her heart, she tries so hard to help me. She comes over every single evening after she finishes her work at the insurance office, and she'll sit right beside me on the sofa in the living room. It's a green velvet sofa, very sturdy, we bought it from Sears back in the eighties and it's held up remarkably well. She sits right there next to me, and she takes my hand in hers. She has such soft hands, she always uses that expensive lavender hand cream she gets in her stocking every Christmas, so she always smells like flowers. She just holds my hand, and she sits quietly with me. 

And doctor... I look at her, and I know I love her. I know it in my head. She's my daughter, and I've loved her since the very day she was born. But... I cannot feel the warmth of it inside me at all. Not even a tiny bit. It's just a cold fact in my brain now, like knowing two and two make four. The actual feeling—that warmth and comfort you're supposed to get when your child holds your hand and tries to be there for you—it's just entirely missing. I can't feel it. So if I can't even feel the warmth of my own daughter's love when she's sitting right beside me holding my hand, I certainly can't find a drop of pleasure in a crossword puzzle or anything else.

doctor.intent: Determine the presence of marked diminished interest in activities
doctor.question: Are there any activities that you used to do before your grandson's passing that you have completely stopped doing since then?

target_item.name: Functional Impairment
target_item.manifestation: I have stopped going to my walking club and I cannot bring myself to help with the funeral repast planning, even though those are the very people and duties my family depends on me for.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about activities I have completely stopped doing since the traumatic event, which directly relates to my functional impairment, specifically stopping my walking club and helping with funeral repast planning.

patient.answer:
Activities I've stopped doing... well, yes, I suppose there are. I used to be quite involved, you know. I had my routine. I used to go to my walking club every Tuesday and Thursday morning. We called ourselves the "Silver Steppers"—there were about six of us ladies from the neighborhood, and we'd meet at nine o'clock sharp at the entrance to Centennial Park. I always wore my good New Balance shoes, the gray ones with the extra arch support because of that left knee of mine. We'd walk the paved loop around the duck pond, and then we'd stop for coffee at the little diner on Main Street. But since... well, since the news about my grandson, I have completely stopped going. I haven't been once. Mildred called my landline twice last week to ask where I was, but I just let the answering machine take it. I just sit and listen to her voice echoing out of the little speaker, and I can't even bring myself to pick up the receiver. 

And it's not just the walking club. It's... well, it's the things that actually matter right now. The funeral repast planning. Usually, when someone in our church community passes away, I am the very first one on the telephone tree. I'm the one who organizes the casseroles, I make sure someone brings the paper plates—the sturdy ones, mind you, not those flimsy white ones that collapse the second you put a scoop of macaroni salad on them. I've been doing it for decades. 

But for my own grandson... my family is depending on me to help plan the repast after his service. It's what we do, it's tradition to gather everyone and have some sandwiches and coffee, maybe some of those little lemon bars my sister used to bake. My daughter asked if I could just call the bakery to order the rolls, just one small task to help get things organized. But doctor, I cannot bring myself to do it. I can't pick up the phone. I can't write down a list of who is bringing what. I know these are the very people and duties my family depends on me for, especially right now when everyone is struggling so much, but I just can't do any of it. I just sit in my floral armchair while they try to figure it all out without me. I've just stopped doing... well, everything, really.

Well, doctor, like I was just trying to explain a moment ago... no. No, not even the small things. I really have to emphasize this, because it's the very thing that frightened me enough to come in and see you today.

doctor.intent: determine the presence of significant weight loss
doctor.question: Have you lost a significant amount of weight since your grandson passed away?

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about weight loss, which is not covered by any of the available symptom profiles.

patient.answer:
Weight? Oh... well, no. No, I haven't lost a significant amount of weight. Or, well, I don't think I have. I haven't stepped on the scale, to be perfectly honest with you. The scale is in the upstairs bathroom—the one with the peach tiles that my husband put in back in 1978, he did all the grouting himself, you know. But I haven't been up those stairs in... well, since the police came to the door that night. I've just been sleeping on the downstairs sofa, the green velvet one I mentioned earlier. 

But as for my weight... I suppose my clothes still fit the same. My slacks aren't falling down or anything like that. It's funny you ask, though, because it's not as if I'm eating normally. I'm really not. My daughter brings over these Tupperware containers—the good heavy plastic ones with the snap lids—filled with casseroles and soups, and she tries to get me to eat. She'll heat up a bowl of chicken noodle soup and set it right on the coffee table in front of me, and she'll say, "Mom, you have to keep your strength up." And I look at it, and I know I should eat it, but I just... I don't have the appetite for it. I might manage a few spoonfuls just to appease her, so she doesn't worry quite so much, but it all just tastes like ash in my mouth anyway. 

But no, despite all that, I haven't noticed any real change in my weight. I suppose when you're just sitting in an armchair all day, staring at the wall and not moving, you don't really burn off what little you do manage to swallow. So, no, doctor, I wouldn't say I've lost a significant amount of weight. Not that I've noticed, anyway.

doctor.intent: determine the presence of marked diminished interest in activities
doctor.question: Are there things you used to do before your grandson's passing that you now find you have no interest in doing at all?

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about a loss of interest in previously enjoyed activities (diminished interest), which is a symptom of depression but is not included in the patient's acute stress disorder symptom profile. The patient's profile includes inability to experience positive emotions, which was already addressed.

patient.answer:
Well, like I was saying just a moment ago about the walking club and the funeral repast planning... it's all of it, doctor. Everything. I suppose you could say I've lost interest, but it feels... it feels heavier than just losing interest, if that makes any sense. It's not like when I lost interest in knitting back in the nineties after my arthritis started acting up, where I just didn't want to bother with the needles anymore. This is different. 

I used to love tending to my garden, you know. I have—or I had, I suppose—these beautiful rose bushes out front. The Peace roses, the big yellow ones with the pink edges. I used to go out there every single morning with my gardening shears and my thick leather gloves, the ones my husband bought me for our fortieth anniversary, and I'd spend an hour just pruning and deadheading and making sure the Japanese beetles weren't getting to the leaves. But now... I can see them through the front window from where I sit on the sofa. I can see the weeds growing up around the base of the birdbath, and the roses are starting to drop their petals because it's been so dry, and I just... I don't care. I look at them, and I know I should go out there with the watering can, but the thought of actually doing it, the thought of caring whether they live or die, it just feels completely impossible. 

And my crossword puzzles, too. I used to do the Sunday puzzle in pen. Every Sunday morning, with a cup of Earl Grey tea. Now the newspapers are just piling up on the porch, wrapped in their little plastic sleeves. The neighbor boy, Tommy, he brings them up to the door for me so they don't sit at the end of the driveway, but I don't even open them. I have absolutely no desire to look at a crossword puzzle. I have no desire to do anything. It's just as I said before, doctor, I just sit there. The interest is just... gone. Completely gone.

doctor.intent: Determine if the patient has a depressed mood
doctor.question: Do you feel depressed most of the day, every day, since your grandson passed away?

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about feeling depressed most of the day, which is a symptom of depressed mood. The patient's symptom profile includes the inability to experience positive emotions (S076), but does not specifically include depressed mood.

patient.answer:
Depressed? I... I don't know if depressed is the right word for it, doctor. I'm not sure. When I think of being depressed, I think of my sister, Helen. Back in the eighties, she went through a terrible depression after she lost her job at the bank—she was a teller there for twenty-five years, you know, and then they brought in those new machines and let her go. She would cry all day, just weep and weep, and talk about how awful everything was. 

But I'm not... I'm not crying like that. Not most of the day, anyway. It's more like what I was trying to explain about the roses and the crossword puzzles. It's just this heavy, awful blankness. It's not that I'm sitting there feeling deeply sad in a way that makes me want to sob, it's just that I don't feel anything at all. It's like I'm hollowed out. Like an old gourd that's been left out in the sun too long, just a dry shell with nothing left inside. 

So, I don't know if that's depression. I really don't. Is that what depression is? Just... sitting on a green velvet sofa staring at the wall, not caring if the sun comes up or goes down? Because if that's what it is, then I suppose I am. But if depression means feeling sad and crying all the time, like Helen did, then no. I'm just... empty. Every day, all day long. Just empty.

patient.answer:
Well, doctor... didn't we just talk about this? With the roses and the crossword puzzles? I feel like I just answered this. I mean, yes, it's exactly what I was just saying. I have no interest. None at all. 

I used to love those things, like I told you. The gardening, the puzzles on Sunday morning with my Earl Grey tea... but now, it's just nothing. It's like I was saying about the garden, seeing the weeds grow up around the birdbath and just not caring. It's all just... gone. The interest is just completely gone. I really don't know how else to explain it, doctor. It's just exactly what I said a minute ago.

doctor.intent: Determine the duration of the patient's emotional numbness
doctor.question: For how long have you been feeling this emotional numbness and inability to feel love for your daughter?

target_item.name: Duration
target_item.manifestation: This has been going on for the 6 days since my grandson was killed outside the community center.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking for the duration of the symptoms ('For how long have you been feeling this emotional numbness...'). This directly maps to the 'Duration' item in the symptom profile.

patient.answer:
Well, doctor... it's been exactly six days. Six days since... since it happened. Since he was killed right outside the community center. 

I remember it was a Tuesday. It was a Tuesday afternoon, and it had been raining earlier in the day, just a light drizzle, the kind that makes the pavement smell like wet dust. I was sitting on that same green velvet sofa I told you about, looking out the window at the roses, thinking I wouldn't need to water them because of the rain. And then the phone rang. It was the old rotary phone I keep in the hallway, the one with the loud, jangling bell that always makes me jump a little. 

It was my daughter, Sarah. She was hysterical, just screaming into the receiver, and I couldn't understand what she was saying at first. I kept telling her, "Sarah, slow down, sweetheart, slow down, Mother can't understand you." And then she finally got the words out. She said... she said there had been a shooting. Right outside the community center where he played basketball on Tuesdays. He was just walking out the door, doctor. Just walking out the door with his gym bag over his shoulder, the blue one with the white stripe that I bought him for his birthday last year. 

Ever since that phone call, ever since that exact moment when the receiver slipped out of my hand and hit the hardwood floor—it left a little dent, right near the baseboard, I saw it yesterday when I was just staring at the wall—ever since then, it's just been... this. This terrible, heavy nothingness. I look at Sarah when she comes over to check on me, and I know she's hurting, I know she just lost her boy, her only boy, and I know I should want to hold her and comfort her. I know I should feel that deep, overwhelming love a mother feels when her child is in pain. But I just... I look at her, and I feel nothing. Just that empty gourd feeling. Six days of it. Six long, empty days.

patient.answer:
More than just grieving? I... I don't know what you mean by that, doctor. I really don't. What else could it possibly be? 

I mean, I'm eighty-four years old. I've lived a long time, and I've seen a lot of things. I've lost people before. I lost my husband, Arthur, fifteen years ago this November. He had a bad heart, you see, and we always knew it was coming, but it still hurt. Oh, it hurt terribly. I cried for months. I couldn't even look at his armchair—the brown leather one by the fireplace—without bursting into tears. But that felt like grief. It felt like a sharp, agonizing pain right in the center of my chest. 

This... this is different. But it's still about him. It's still about my grandson. It's all tied up in that phone call, and the rain on the windowpane, and the dent in the floorboards. I don't see how it could be related to anything else. I don't have anything else going on in my life, doctor. I'm just an old woman who putters around her garden and does the Sunday crossword. Or, well, I used to be. Now I'm just an old woman who sits on a green velvet sofa and stares at the wall. 

So, no, I don't think it's anything else. I don't even know what else it could be. It's just... it's just this terrible thing that happened six days ago, and everything stopped. The whole world just stopped turning. Why would you think it's something else? Is there something else wrong with me? Because I can't imagine anything worse than this... this hollow feeling. It's just all about him. It has to be.

doctor.intent: Determine the presence of anhedonia
doctor.question: Are you able to experience pleasure or enjoyment from any activities or things?

target_item.name: Inability_Positive_Emotions
target_item.manifestation: I came in because since my grandson was killed, my daughter can sit right beside me holding my hand and I know I love her, but I cannot feel the warmth of it inside me at all.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about the ability to experience pleasure or enjoyment, which directly maps to the persistent inability to experience positive emotions.

patient.answer:
Doctor, I feel like... well, I feel like we keep going around in circles about this. It's just like I was trying to explain about the garden, and the crosswords, and... and my daughter, Sarah. It all comes back to the same terrible thing. 

You ask about pleasure or enjoyment, and I... I just don't have it. I came in here today, to this office, because ever since my grandson was killed six days ago, everything has just gone completely cold. I was sitting with Sarah just yesterday. She came over in the afternoon, bringing some sort of casserole in a glass dish that I know I'll never eat. She sat right down beside me on that green velvet sofa, and she took my hand in hers. Her hands were so warm, doctor, just like they were when she was a little girl and we'd walk to the park together. 

I looked at her sitting there, crying over her boy, and I know in my head that I love her. She's my daughter, my only child, of course I love her. But... I couldn't feel it. I couldn't feel the warmth of that love inside me at all. It was just... nothing. Just that same hollow, empty feeling I've had since the phone rang. If I can't even feel the love for my own grieving daughter when she's holding my hand, how could I possibly find pleasure in a crossword puzzle or a blooming rose? It's all just gone, doctor. Every bit of warmth, every bit of joy, it's just vanished completely.
